prompt: A manager asks a new engineer to 'make the dashboard better'. The engineer starts by asking which users complain and what they are trying to do.
tells: asking which users complain and what they are trying to do
why: A vague request needs its real goal pinned down before any code.
trap: Asking here isn't being stuck; it's defining the work.

prompt: In a system design interview, the candidate is told 'design a URL shortener' and first asks how many users, how many links a day and whether links expire.
tells: first asks how many users, how many links a day and whether links expire
why: Pin down scale and requirements before drawing boxes.
trap: Numbers come up, but no one is measuring a running system.

prompt: A ticket says 'add CSV export'. Before building, the engineer asks the requester what they will do with the file, and learns they only need a total that the page could show.
tells: asks the requester what they will do with the file
why: Asking about the underlying need found a simpler solution.
trap: The result is less code, but the move was asking first.

prompt: Two days into a task, an engineer realizes no one agreed on what 'done' means. She writes down acceptance criteria and checks them with the product manager.
tells: no one agreed on what 'done' means
why: Agree what success looks like before building more.
trap: Writing is involved, but it's requirements, not a design doc.

prompt: In a coding interview, before writing code, the candidate asks whether the input can be empty, can have duplicates and how large it can get.
tells: asks whether the input can be empty, can have duplicates and how large it can get
why: Clear up the problem's limits before solving.
trap: Edge cases also matter in testing, but this happens before any code exists.

prompt: A spec line can be read two ways, and each would take a week. Instead of picking one, the engineer sends both readings to the author and asks which is meant.
tells: sends both readings to the author and asks which is meant
why: Settle ambiguity in the requirement before spending a week.
trap: It's not a quick reversible pick; a wrong guess costs a week.
